name: EAGLE (EAGLE-1/2/3 speculative decoding)
notable_features: Feature-level speculative decoding: instead of a separate draft LM, EAGLE trains a lightweight autoregressive head over the target model's own top-layer features. EAGLE-1 reframed speculative sampling as a feature-uncertainty problem (arXiv:2401.15077); EAGLE-2 uses dynamic draft trees (arXiv:2406.16858); EAGLE-3 removes the feature-prediction constraint and uses training-time test (arXiv:2503.01840, NeurIPS'25)
EAGLE-3 is lossless in the paper's terms - it does not change the target model's output distribution
Composable with other acceleration work: the README lists vLLM, DeepSpeed, Mamba, FlashAttention, quantization and hardware optimisation as combinable
The README reports a 2x speedup on gpt-fast as the headline
Support spans vLLM (PR 16937), SGLang speculative decoding, vllm-project/speculators and Intel LLM Library for PyTorch - i.e. the paper's implementation is now consumed by other projects
The README recommends SGLang's SpecForge for out-of-the-box EAGLE-3 training as of 2025-07-23, which is the clearest signal that the mainstream path moved elsewhere
hardware_caveats: LICENSE IS NOT A STANDARD OSI LICENSE. The GitHub API reports spdx_id NOASSERTION and license name 'Other' for this repo. Do not assume permissive terms for commercial use - read LICENSE directly. license is left null here rather than guessed

Requires a trained EAGLE head per model and per draft length, so it is not a drop-in for stock checkpoints. EAGLE-3 heads for specific models are published separately and version-lock to the base model
CUDA in practice: a pure-Python repo (874126 bytes of Python and nothing else per the language breakdown) that depends on the host framework and its kernels. No ROCm, Metal or Vulkan path documented
No GitHub releases at all, so there is no versioned artefact to pin - you install from a commit

The project itself now points elsewhere for the mainstream workflow (SpecForge with SGLang, vllm-project/speculators with vLLM). This repo is the paper implementation and reference training code, not the recommended deployment path

Acceptance rate is the whole game: a 2x claim is a vendor claim on the author's own models and hardware with no methodology table in the README. Speedups shrink on small models and on high-temperature sampling
NOT deprecated, unlike [[niche-medusa]] - last push 2026-02-20 and it is the live reference for a technique the field adopted. But it is a reference implementation now, not a product
best_for: Reading the reference implementation of the speculative-decoding technique that the field actually standardised on
Understanding why feature-level drafting beats token-level drafting, and what training-time test changes about the loss surface
Training EAGLE-3 heads with SpecForge + SGLang, or serving them through vLLM's speculators plugin
avoid_for: Production deployment without reading the LICENSE - NOASSERTION is a real risk, not a formality
Drop-in speedups on stock checkpoints, which need per-model trained heads
Non-CUDA hosts, and any workflow that needs a supported release rather than a commit
notes: The speculative-decoding record that survived. Contrast with [[niche-medusa]]: EAGLE kept being implemented on (last push 2026-02-20 vs Medusa's 2024-06-25), produced the three-paper lineage that the serving stacks cite, and got absorbed into vLLM, SGLang, vllm-project/speculators and Intel's ip-llm. arXiv titles/dates for 2401.15077, 2406.16858, 2503.01840 and the NeurIPS'25 acceptance all verified via the arXiv API; all repo metadata from the GitHub API on 2026-10-03.
